"One shot, one thrill."

Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts is a tactical shooter that delivers a satisfying sniping experience for fans of stealth and precision gameplay. If you're into planning your shots, scouting your environment, and executing missions with surgical accuracy, this game hits the mark.

Pros:

    🎯 Tight sniping mechanics: Bullet drop, wind, and breathing control add realism without being frustrating. Nailing long-distance headshots feels amazing.

    🌲 Beautiful environments: From snow-covered Siberian wilderness to industrial compounds, the levels are well-designed and immersive.

    🔍 Contract-style missions: Each map has multiple objectives and encourages replayability. You can approach missions in several ways—stealth, action, or a bit of both.

    🧠 Strategic gameplay: This isn’t run-and-gun. You'll need to plan routes, use your gadgets (like the drone or mask), and pick your targets carefully.

    🕵️ Silent approach is rewarded: The game encourages smart, quiet play and gives you the tools to be creative.

At the Summer Sale price of $8 CDN, It's hard to dislike. The actual sniping mechanics are very well done, and highly enjoyable, easily the primary thing I enjoy in this game.

First off: DO NOT buy this game for $40 CDN, period.

Firstly, the new player experience sucks. it's pretty clear that nobody thought to playtest the current state of the game from a new player's experience, because fundamental equipment options are not explained to you in game. you WILL be searching "Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts" repeatedly on google to figure out things such as
-Which guns are compatible with which special ammo types?
-Which guns can be suppressed?
the game's blink-and-you'll-miss-it tutorial gives you a decent understanding of the fundamental equipment, but then no guidance on how you'd actually *use* that equipment for contracts. "These special ammo types are important, but also not every gun works with every ammo, and you can only see the details of each weapon AFTER you buy it."

I found myself turning the bullet cam almost all the way down because the duration it takes is a bit long in the tooth, frankly, it's no Sniper Elite X-Ray.

I don't really take issue with the graphics, i don't really mind the "look" of CryEngine games, something I see people chide often. The graphics serve the game just fine. I will however say that the polish of certain game aspects is pretty lackluster, and painfully reminiscent of ancient titles. Oddly enough, the way the interactions, animations, and camera whiplash during said animations, and general jankiness actually remind me of Far Cry 2. Which is impressively annoying given that Far Cry 2 runs on a forked version of CryEngine 1, and came out over a decade prior.

Picking up bodies is really frustrating because it's really evident when you "drop" the body, it's just spawning a ragdoll midair, where it collides with something and goes everywhere except where you actually intended to drop it. I find myself repeatedly picking up the same body to nudge it further out of sightlines.

However, these are all relatively minor compared to my biggest issue with this game. Save persistence. 

Clearly, the game is capable of remembering details like "you killed that guard" "you shot that breaker panel" but for same insane reason corpses DO NOT PERSIST in a stealth based sniping game. Thankfully, ammo caches are abundant, so you don't *need* the bodies for ammo, but even on the hardest difficulty, it means there's no punishment for failure. You'll die, and half the time it plonks a checkpoint in the middle of what you were doing, except there's no alarm, the bodies that could raise the alarm are gone, and everyone forgets that you just blew their leader's head clean off thirty seconds prior.

The biggest punishment for dying is that the game makes you live with yourself for getting a free pass after you screwed up, or you magically got spotted by someone who wasn't using binoculars instantly from several hundred meters away. That one does happen periodically.

I enjoy FPS games with an element of stealth, so I really wanted to like this game. Sadly, after 8 hours and 3 missions, I uninstalled the game. I wish I could get a refund, but apparently there is a 2-gameplay-hour limit. I had hoped that, if I just finished the first mission, it would get better...but it didn't.

First, some things I did like:
-The gunplay is good. The shooting mechanics are fun, and reward practice.
-There are multiple ways to approach objectives.
-The story and its role in the objectives is interesting.
-Pretty graphics. Detailed character models.
-Detailed NPC dialogue.

What I didn't like:
-Omniscient enemies. If you shoot someone with a suppressor from 400 m. away, and someone sees them die, they immediately know where you are.
-Enemies have godlike aim. That enemy 400 m. away can shoot you reliably with his AK-47.
-Gadgets are useless, because they aren't nearly as lethal or effective as you would think, and trying to use them will immediately alert all the enemies, who will then proceed to murder you.
-No matter how well you plan and sneak, the first time you miss a shot, the entire mission devolves into a machine gun brawl.
-All the side objectives are tedious and boring. There is no good reason for them to exist.
-If you don't want to get caught, you have to spend the ENTIRE mission sneaking around, at half speed, across large maps. I like large maps, but in this game, they just make every mission tedious.
-On some missions, you start surrounded by about a dozen enemies between 10m and 300m away from you, and the second you kill one, they all start shooting, with the aforementioned omniscience and accuracy.

I'm sorry to say that this game just isn't fun. Don't buy it.

It's sort of the modern version of Sniper Elite. The kill cam isn't as cool, and the gameplay is a little more stiff, but it's still a satisfying sniper game with large, open levels and tons of enemies to shoot. Movement can hang up on little things in the environment, and sometimes a jump that should be easy results in your death because the character just doesn't grab the ledge like he is supposed to. Other than those little annoyances, I've not run into anything overly annoying or game breaking. For a sub $10 game on sale, I've already gotten my money's worth and plan to get the sequel when it goes on sale. (STEAM Winter sale FTW!)

There needs to be more simple, generic, just games like this. It's an open level base infiltration game with outposts sprinkled in across the map, their layout is fine, fun to sneak through. As for sniping, it feels like the sequel to this sacrificed the areas you can actually infiltrate to enable the meme over 1000m shots, which is fine for a flash game or a separate type of small side content, but I'd rather have actual levels like here than shooting galleries. If sniping from around 300m doesn't satisfy your sniper fantasy, just zoom out and pretend your range finder shows you 10km, Jesus. 

The AI is fine if you ghost, but if you try to go panther, as in eliminate enemies quietly but hard, leave the bodies etc. then it kinda falls apart. They have very short "suspicious state", and if one enemy gets alerted, suddenly the whole area is, instantly, and they know where you are. Would be much better if, for example, after finding the body, the AI first alarm the nearest squad members, run a search, and then call it in by radio and alert the base. It's gamey, but it's a game, it would give the player a chance to react and correct his mistake instead of loading a badly placed checkpoint.

I really like that this game knows exactly what it is, no patronizing, no deep message, no forced gaming tropes like open world, the devs clearly learned from SGW3 and found the type of game they are comfortable with making. Thematically enemy installations are just soldier camps and post-soviet bases but there is a suprising amount of soul here. Each level has some nice vistas and clearly takes place in a different region, with different weather and time of day that suits the area best. First level is cool, mountains at night, a slight blizzard and northern lights in the sky.

Should be way longer though, same as the sequel. Devs claim it has replayability like Hitman, but that's BS, after running a map once you've seen every path you can take, no reason to replay, first time is nice though.

I recommend this game, but only, and only when there's a discount.

It's buggy, and there's some issues that I faced with the gameplay.

The colliding physics is a bit off. For instance, when you are trying to move up, just because of a little small bump, poor seeker suddenly forgets how to lift his leg up a lil more to move over that obstacle. I got detected and died so many times because of this nonsense and you're going to have a lot of it because the terrain you're on is mostly undulating. 

Sometimes death from above also doesn't activate when it seems like it should. No reason why you can't do it regardless when an enemy is in a corner but hey, apparently, sitting in a corner grants you  immunity from death from above.

This game has some infuriating bugs like your cursor can no longer right click to mark a checkpoint or even do anything. Your game isn't hanged. Your cursor still moves as you will it but nothing will happen despite what you click in the menu. The only way to get around this is to restart.

Another would be teleporting you to the other side of the AO when you reload a checkpoint.

Here's another bug (maybe a bug, maybe not) but there's a certain character that you're told to interrogate cos it might be helpful so even though I had clear shots, I decided not to kill that guy until I had a chance to speak with him. But no. After many tries (cos I am terrible at stealth), I was awarded with the usual "Where's are the supplies?" interrogation lines. Yeah, sure. Real helpful. I thought by interrogating him I might get a little more info the spice up the story, but that's all she wrote. Supplies monkey trucker.

Anyway, it's still not utterly a bad game. There's nice futuristic concepts, and the difficult stealth. Takedown animations are brutal but awesome. Gunplay feels nice with the sniper, and assault rifle. Pistols feel a bit off, I feel, but it's functional and i did have fun with it.

The arsenal here is limited but each sniper rifle offers something different. More ammo or less ammo? Semi-auto or bolt action. There's tiers too ranging from your 7.62 caliber to .338 lapua magnum to the big ol' 50 cal. There's special ammo that you could also equip. For secondary and sidearms, I mainly equipped the AK-12 and HK Mk.23 without silencers cos if I had to go loud, I'd rather go all the way. I'm not sure if suppressors reduce damage in this game either so I decided to do without it altogether. Only my sniper would have a suppressor.

You've got skills that you can unlock to customise to suit your playstyle.

There is a nice range of utilities. From frag grenades, flashbangs, bouncing betties, to anti-tank mines, gas mines/grenades, decoys, adrenaline, med kits etc.

On a whim and bored of my library, I decided to buy SGW3 on sale as it was dirt cheap. I poured through the game obsessively in a few days. Sure, it was buggy. Sure, it had all the flaws of the open world Ubisoft genre. But there was was something so satisfying about the gunplay that it kept me hooked despite it's ups and downs. And yet, there was also something else I couldn't quite place my thumb on that elevated the game to great heights during certain points.

After beating it, I decided to buy SGWC1 and hoo boy. I think the devs finally realized what they're good at.

In a couple words: map design.

Ya'll have some of the best map design I've ever seen in games. The gunplay is still satisfying, and I highly enjoy not being forced to play a specific way (with the exception of the challenges).

But the MAP DESIGN.

In other games, areas feel like cheap one dimensional areas with buildings placed from prebaked assets. There's often times only a couple of ways into the location. Enemies don't pop-in until the player is close, and then they stand around and wait for the player to kill them.

In this game, every area is a puzzle, a labyrinth waiting to be mapped out. Most enemies have a wide patrol range, and their paths are very dynamic.

I haven't even beaten SGWC1 yet but am thoroughly enjoying it. I went ahead and bought SGWC2 ahead of time to support the devs.

[h1]Not quite Sniper Elite, but pretty close.[/h1]

The first of the five big open-world-missions in Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts was admittedly rough. The second one went significantly smoother, and in the third one i was sniping dudes from 300 meter distances like it was nothing and had a blast for the remainder of the game.

Don't know if you could call the sniping mechanics and physics realistic (Sniper Elite seems to be slightly more so, it seems to me), but it is a bit tough to learn how to use your scope properly and it will take one or two missions until you get the feeling for it, so I guess you could call this a proper sniper simulation. Anyways, even on the easiest difficulty setting the game is absolutely no cakewalk and if you are one of the impatient kind who just tries to go in all Rambo, running and gunning your way through, you'll get your ass kicked. SGWC is more of a thinking man's game where you have to plan ahead and try to stay as stealthy as possible.

Unfortunately, the mostly fair challenge flips into unfair territory now and then, because the enemy AI is dumb as dogsh*t and they have to compensate their lack of intelligence by having impossible accuracy: Those b*st*rds can hit you with a common assault rifle from 200 meters away, even if you're prone in high grass on top of a hill.

But that's basically the only thing to really complain about. The rest ist just nitpicking. The gore effects are slightly exagerated (this is the kind of game where you can take a half face off with a small 9mm pistol), but overall the presentation is solid. The "story" is far from a masterpiece, but at least it gives you a decent enough explanation why you are doing what you are doing. Five missions seem a bit short and the replay value is relatively low if you are not a completionist, but even on the easiest difficulty the longest of the missions can take up to 3 hours so you'll be occupied for at least 8 to 10 hours if you just focus on the main missions alone.

In the end SGWC is a fun game for people who like their First-Person-Shooters with a balanced mix of casual gameplay and challenging realism and a good dose of stealth on top. If the historical WWII setting of Sniper Elite is not for you, the Sniper Ghost Warrior series is the next best thing.

There are two requirements for you to better enjoy Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts: The first would be for the player to see this game as something a bit different from the traditional Sniper Elite games as well older Sniper Ghost Warrior games. The second requirement is patience. Excel at these two and you will be having some fun with the game.

With only 5 maps for you to play, at first it seems short but we are talking about big maps with 5 or more different objectives scattered across the map. How you approach it is entirely up to you. The tutorial is brief and short so don’t be shy to repeat it if you did not get aiming on your first try. I tried to go full stealth at the start but later on some sections I was using all the possible firepower at my will. It’s not the way I wanted or intended to play the game but with some issues with checkpoints and a not-so-clever AI, it made me switch playstyles. Still, there was fun to be had. The game looks good and plays well in general, perhaps a bit of optimization could help not push my hardware so much but I’ve managed just fine.

[h1]The gameplay flow features stand out more than the story[/h1]
As my first foray into the franchise, Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts lets me dive in on what it means being a covert operative in the modern era; set amidst the backdrop of a conflicted Siberian nation.

One of the game's strengths is its ability to introduce fresh challenges in each level. Whether I am tasked with eliminating targets from a distance (with a satisfying slo-mo camera angle to boot) or navigating close-quarters combat situations, Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts does a good job keeping me on my toes. The constant need to adapt myself in large maps keeps the gameplay engaging.

The inclusion of unlockable traits is a welcome addition. These traits allows me to customize my character's abilities and approach missions in different ways. Normally I thrive in going the stealthy path and taking out my targets from a safe distance (for the namesake of the franchise) but it does open for players preferring a more aggressive playstyle. That's thanks to the ability to tailor your skills, which adds depth to the game.

The game excels as well at providing a sense of accomplishment through its mission structure. Completing objectives and missions yields points for you to spend on your personal upgrades and inventory, adding replay value to the mission for players to unlock further or playing through missions through a different angle. However, as much as story intrigue goes, the overarching plot of fighting against a separatist nation in Siberia lacks the memorability for me after a while.

On a side-note, Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts suffers from an occasional issue where movement can become stuck during gameplay. This recurring glitch is rather counter-productive when you try to find a different path through the terrain, making it a drawback for the flow.

Overall, the game's varied challenges, customizable traits, and rewarding mission structure contribute to its appeal for stealth and sniping game fans. Movement issues and shallow story aside, I hope to see with the sequel, being up in my backlog, the improvements to enhance and add further stability and substance into it.

One of the most defining aspects of "Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts" is its mission-based structure, which is a departure from the open-world format of its predecessor, "Sniper Ghost Warrior 3." This change is a double-edged sword; while it provides more focused and well-designed levels, it also limits the sense of freedom that players may have enjoyed in the previous game. Each mission, or "contract," is set in a distinct, semi-open environment with a variety of objectives to complete. These can range from assassinating high-value targets to sabotaging enemy operations and collecting intelligence. The game encourages a methodical approach, rewarding players who take the time to scout the area, identify enemy positions, and plan their attacks accordingly. The sniping mechanics are the core of the gameplay experience. Wind direction, bullet drop, and distance all affect the trajectory of your shots, requiring players to carefully consider their positioning and timing.
The game includes a "mask mode" that enhances the player's tactical awareness, allowing for tagging enemies and spotting environmental hazards. While sniping from a distance is the primary focus, players often need to navigate through enemy-infested areas. This necessitates a combination of stealth tactics, such as using suppressed weapons, avoiding detection, and utilizing distractions. Direct combat is less encouraged due to the protagonist's vulnerability in close-quarters, emphasizing the importance of staying hidden and striking from afar. Players have access to a variety of gadgets, including drones, remote sniper turrets, and various types of ammunition. These tools add layers of strategy and offer multiple ways to approach objectives.
Customizable loadouts allow players to tailor their equipment to suit their preferred playstyle. "Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts" boasts impressive visuals, particularly in its depiction of the harsh Siberian landscape. The game features a mix of dense forests, snow-covered mountains, and industrial complexes, all rendered with a high level of detail. The environments are beautifully crafted, with dynamic weather effects and realistic lighting that enhance the immersive experience. Snowfall, fog, and rain not only add to the atmosphere but also impact visibility and gameplay.
Character models and animations are generally well-done, although some minor glitches and clipping issues can occasionally break immersion. The sound design is another strong point. The echo of a sniper rifle firing across a snowy expanse, the muffled sounds of footsteps in deep snow, and the ambient noises of the environment all contribute to a highly immersive experience.
Voice acting is competent, if not particularly standout. The dialogue and mission briefings are clear and functional, but they lack the emotional depth and nuance found in some other narrative-driven games. The narrative of "Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts" is relatively straightforward. Set in a near-future Siberia, the game unfolds against a backdrop of political  Players take on the role of a paid contract sniper known as "Seeker," who works for a shadowy organization. The story revolves around completing contracts that destabilize the local power structure and eliminate key figures.
The plot is delivered through mission briefings, in-game communications, and occasional cutscenes. While serviceable, the story lacks depth and character development, serving more as a framework for the gameplay than a compelling narrative journey. The setting itself is rich with detail, providing a believable and immersive world. The game's environments tell stories of their own, with abandoned facilities, war-torn villages, and heavily guarded compounds all contributing to the atmosphere. The political backdrop and regional conflicts add a layer of realism and context to the player's actions, even if the main narrative thread remains fairly generic. "Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts" offers a good amount of replayability, thanks to its open-ended mission structure and multiple paths to achieving objectives. Each contract can be approached in numerous ways, encouraging players to experiment with different strategies and equipment loadouts. This non-linear approach makes revisiting missions enjoyable and rewarding. The game includes additional challenges and side objectives that provide extra content and incentives for thorough exploration and tactical creativity.While the main campaign can be completed in around 10-15 hours, the various challenges, collectibles, and higher difficulty levels extend the game's lifespan. However, once all objectives are achieved, there is limited post-game content beyond replaying missions for higher scores.

"Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts" is a solid entry in the tactical shooter genre, offering a satisfying blend of precision sniping, stealth mechanics, and strategic gameplay. Its mission-based structure allows for focused and well-crafted levels, even if it sacrifices some of the freedom of its predecessor. The game excels in creating an immersive atmosphere with its detailed environments and sound design, though its narrative remains relatively shallow. For fans of sniping and stealth games, "Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts" provides a rewarding and challenging experience that emphasizes careful planning and execution. While it may not revolutionize the genre, it stands out as a competent and enjoyable game that will keep players engaged with its tactical depth and immersive world.

Unlike a traditional stealth game focused on keeping yourself out of view or secretly taking out unsuspecting foes at close range, in sniping games like Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts you’re better off keeping your distance. It’s all about reveling in the careful, precise sniping that requires methodical movements and attention to detail. Contracts, in particular, is slow at times and the obligatory escapes can be a bit boring, but the long stretches of downtime are often punctuated by exhilarating explosions of gore that make it worthwhile.

A mostly inconsequential story about oil companies, international espionage, and vague politics loosely connects 25 contract objectives across five enormous sandbox-style maps. A forgettable prologue explains why it’s morally okay to assassinate each target for money. It was nice getting some context for why I’m being asked to murder dozens of people, but at the end of the day the game is called Sniper and it gives me a long gun with slow-mo powers so I don’t need much other motivation beyond that. From there it’s just a matter of completing your objectives and cashing the check. Sometimes you’re also hacking computer terminals, planting bombs, or stealing intel – all basic stuff.
Since the levels are so huge and mostly free of restrictions, it didn’t feel necessary or interesting to pay attention to the story. What makes completing a contract challenging, though, is the scope of the maps. They’re staggering in size and require fast-travel to get around in any reasonable amount of time. They range from urban coastlines full of cargo ships lining the harbor with massive oil rigs spread about, to enormous fortresses built into the side of glaciers, all the way to private mansions tucked away between forests. There’s a lot of variety, both visually and in terms of the environments forcing you to adapt your approach based on terrain and layout.
There is a litany of gadgets at your disposal, too. You can spend cash you earn from completing contracts to unlock powerful new guns and upgrades for your suit and visor, such as the ability to spot climbable objects and traps or zoom your binoculars farther to tag more enemies. Plus, there’s an assortment of gadgetry – everything from grenades and C4 to drones that help mark targets, and even remote-controlled sniper turrets that can fire at enemies on your command. Using these to line up simultaneous kill shots is a lot of fun and all of the gadgets really open up the ways to complete contracts. Tagging enemies with the drone, setting up the turret on the edge of a cliff, ziplining down to enemies, then dropping tagged enemies with your turret just by pressing a button on your approach feels really powerful.
Completing all of the base-level contracts on the five maps can take around 12 hours if you’re a capable marksman. Beyond the core objectives there are some side challenges to offer replayability (like completing contracts without alerting enemies, getting chain kills rapidly, or completing all contracts on a map without loading a checkpoint) but nothing all that interesting to me. There wasn’t enough incentive to care much personally – once I checked off the contracts I moved on without hesitation.

Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts is nothing short of a masterpiece, an instant classic crafted by the brilliant minds at CI Games that seamlessly blends gritty realism with a tantalizing touch of fantasy. From the moment you step into the boots of the enigmatic sniper, you’re thrust into a world that feels both authentic and exhilaratingly larger-than-life. CI Games has truly outdone themselves, delivering a title that elevates the sniper genre to new heights with its impeccable design and captivating gameplay.
The realism is striking—every shot requires precision, patience, and a keen understanding of your environment. Wind speed, distance, and bullet drop aren’t just mechanics; they’re immersive elements that make you feel like a true marksman stalking the shadows. The attention to detail in the weapon handling and the sprawling, beautifully rendered Siberian landscapes is jaw-dropping, grounding the experience in a way that few games manage to achieve. It’s as if CI Games studied the art of sniping and translated it into a digital love letter for tactical enthusiasts.
Yet, what sets Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts apart is how it sprinkles in just the right amount of fantasy to keep things thrilling. You’re not just a soldier—you’re a ghost, a near-mythical figure weaving through contracts with gadgets and skills that push the boundaries of what’s possible. The ability to tag enemies with high-tech scopes, execute jaw-dropping slow-motion kills, and navigate missions with a freedom that feels almost superhuman adds a layer of excitement that perfectly complements the realism. It’s this fusion that makes every mission feel like a cinematic blockbuster, where you’re both the director and the star.
CI Games has struck gold with this title, proving they’re a studio with a vision that resonates. The pacing is spot-on, the replayability is endless thanks to the contract system, and the satisfaction of nailing a 500-meter headshot is unmatched. Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts isn’t just a game—it’s a testament to how a developer can take a niche concept and turn it into a timeless gem. If you’re looking for a title that balances the raw tension of real-world sniping with the escapist thrill of a fantastical adventure, this is it. An absolute triumph!

This game truly stands out with its remarkable gameplay dynamics. While it predominantly centers around the art of sniping, it introduces elements of stealth into the mix, enhancing the overall experience. The game unfolds through a series of contracts, each teeming with diverse objectives to undertake. Although the total count of missions may not be exceedingly high, the depth of engagement within each mission cluster ensures that you invest a substantial amount of time in exploration and execution. The size of the in-game map is commendable, offering ample terrain to traverse and conquer.

A notable highlight lies in the animation quality, particularly when a well-aimed shot pierces through an enemy's cranium—an aspect executed with satisfying precision. The game's environmental design adds a layer of immersion, such as the authentic sensation of one's character treading on frozen snow, further enhancing the sense of realism.

Completing each contract demands a significant time commitment, and the game intelligently provides the option to pause and resume later, tracking your progress with a percentage indicator. What distinguishes this game is its ability to immerse players so thoroughly in their missions that the surrounding world fades into the background. The freedom to explore within each area, methodically eliminating foes and accomplishing objectives, underscores the game's sense of autonomy. The map design, while not overly elaborate, remains effective, ensuring easy accessibility to your mission goals.

Moreover, securing this game during a sale yielded immense satisfaction, reinforcing the value of the purchase. Without reservation, I extend my enthusiastic recommendation for this title to any gaming enthusiast seeking an engaging and rewarding experience.

Decent game that starts off pretty good with a slight decline as you progress. I expected worse from reviews, anticipating a nest of bugs but encountered relatively few.

Contracts features an intuitive scope on its sniper rifles that aids in showing the impact of wind and distance on the bullet trajectory. Bullet physics is always something that seems to elude my understanding but the way it's implemented here shows the arc the bullet will travel (rather than a floating spot) so that once you have target distance you can reliably hit your mark.

In the earlier levels I enjoyed myself so much I went back to do the challenges such as eliminating targets without raising alarms, only killing named targets etc which is something I rarely am interested in doing. As time went on however I noticed that I was being spotted by targets clearly out of LoS more and more so I was less inclined to tackle the challenges since we clearly weren't playing fair anymore. 
It was a shame since the levels themselves are expansive and visually well designed offering a choice of approaches to snipe from a distance or get close to tackle the various objectives in whichever order you choose. A nice mix of the snowy outdoors and industrial facilities and the latter are very well made (again, shame the enemy developed xray vision as it went on). 

I suppose I should say however that the game is still playable and enjoyable as it progresses, it just seems to become less a matter of ghosting through and more seeing how far you get until your stealth is stolen.

That issue aside it's a game that rewards patience, waiting until targets are isolated before picking them off is a winning strategy. There are a host of gadgets to use for variety but a lot of them end up raising the alarm so are less useful. You can do melee stealth kills and interrogations but you are immobile (and I think not crouched so not benefiting from a lower visual profile) while doing so, it would have been better if you could drag enemies behind cover before choosing what to do with them.

On bugs, encountered a few relatively minor ones:
- Certain flights of stairs would have an odd collision issue if you tried to start going up/down them so you had to jump over the first step.
- One camera was invincible.
- I never got Luring bullets to work at all.
- AP bullets were useful for heavies, not (as the tutorial suggested) piercing any cover.
- There's a multi-takedown skill that only worked when it wanted to, and it rarely wanted to.

I bought a few of the DLCs but I think you could fare just fine without them. 

All in all easily worth a go, especially if it's on sale.

Edit: forgot to mention the scope design.

I wasn't expecting much given the other reviews.  But honestly, it's not bad at all!  I had quite a bit of fun.

The premise is that you're a very good sniper hired by some mysterious guy to take out some bad guys in Siberia.  The game takes place in 5 regions.  Each region has around 5 (give or take) "contracts".  About half of the contracts are to kill someone, and the other half are other objectives such as "destroy the research" or "find the evidence".  Each region also has two "bounties" (optional targets) and "challenges" (such as "do this and that without killing anyone").  In brief, I would describe the game as a "sniping-focused murder sandbox".

I think the gameplay details are pretty well handled.  The length, story, and difficulty were satisfactory.  The upgrade tree is a nice addition.  The challenges are quite interesting, some of them very much baffle me.  

My main praises go to the variety of approaches you can take towards completing the contracts and the design of the bounties.  Although this is explicitly a sniping game, it's clear that the developers intended to allow you to pursue other styles of murdering.  There's a good amount of freedom within the sniping itself as well.  Various targets can be eliminated from multiple vantage points.  As for the bounties, I really enjoyed spotting the rival snipers that overlook the bounty targets.  Sniper vs. sniper action is fun!

My main qualm with the game is that the gameplay loop can get a bit repetitive.  While there are one or two interesting twists in the contracts as the game progresses, I don't find it enough to keep the gameplay fresh over 5 whole regions.  There are also a few minor silly hiccups, from getting stuck on geometry a few times (easily resolved by reloading to the last checkpoint), to a typo here or there, to scout drones magically producing bloodstains when shot.  But I don't find that any of this severely impacts the fun.  I don't think I've ever found myself frustrated at the game, which is a good sign!

The various reviews complain about an omnipotent AI, but I can't relate.  Here is a brief description of how the AI functions, as far as I can tell:  Information between the enemy soldiers travels quite quickly.  When you're in a sniping spot, and an enemy sees another enemy get sniped by you, then word of this spreads rapidly, and pretty soon the entire base is taking cover.  Some enemies will also take out binoculars to look in your direction.  That does not mean, however, that they know exactly where you are.  Only once you are directly spotted (or in other niche scenarios) will the enemies go into combat mode and actually come for you and/or shoot at you.  None of this will happen if your kills are unnoticed, so as long as your kills are done in a well-planned order (which is not easy!), it's possible to clear some bases without the enemies having any idea what hit them.  Of course, what I've just described represents a far more intelligent group of soldiers than what would exist in real life, but I did not at all find these AI mechanics frustrating or more illogical than the usual video-game fare.  I would not say it's perfect, but from a gameplay perspective it seemed acceptable to me.

In sum, I'd give this a 7 or 8 out of 10.  If you're seeing this on sale for 5 bucks, it's definitely worth it.

I do recommend this game as it scratches a fantastic sniping itch that the likes of Sniper Elite have made famous. 

To my mind, the game excels in two key areas:
1) The sniping is fantastic; there is a little skill involved with the wind gauge but it isn't hard to master yet it feels great right up to the last shot. 
2) The level design is intricate enough to allow multiple paths to your objective so it makes you feel more like a smart assassin, planning the kill, rather than a linear assassin (doing what the game tells you). 

There were one or two bugs in my play-through but nothing extreme and certainly nothing that took me out of the experience. 

Lastly, I would counter some of the "angry" reviews that comment on how poor the AI is and that it "immediately knows where you are when you shoot". That is simply not the case. The enemies have three states of existence: passive, alerted, hunting. 

Passive is the default state where they will wander around "guarding". Now, if you take an enemy out from range but someone sees them die or discovers the body, the enemy will become alerted and they will all run for cover. In this state, they get out binoculars and intermittently peak over their cover to try to locate you. If you can kill them all without being spotted, they will simply never shoot you and if you are placed well, you can wipe them all out whilst they are alerted. 

Now, if you are spotted (by binoculars or, more likely, enemy snipers) then they will all converge on your position to try and kill you. The armoured enemies will start shooting in your general direction and whilst it might feel that they have godly aim, they don't and you can easily reposition. 

This is where I would then actively turn to defence to praise because, if you reposition, the enemy will converge on the spot they last knew you to be in and you can effectively give them the slip and start shooting from another location. 

All in all, if you set up well, know your routes of retreat and advance, and fully scan the target zone then you'll have a blast in this game and feel like a god-tier sniper.

Good sniper/stealth game, and supports other play styles, but has some amateurish problems that have not been fixed as the game series produces new versions.

 I love the bullpup suppressed sniper rifle for my midrange style of play - sneaking in and using suppressed equipment to stay stealthy. There are several choices of rifles for different styles of play. Some suppressed always, some optional and some loud and proud.  This of course affects your choice of tactics, close and deadly quiet, midrange flexible approach with suppressed weaponry, or long range and high power death from above! Some interesting gadgets like sensor mines that warn the sniper, gas mines, throwing knives for that close, ultra-quiet approach and so on. There are also the usual combat toys like grenades, smoke grenades, flash bangs and the like. Though I think the game supports stealth better than it does loud and proud. Ammo is short and you constantly have to scrounge. Open combat is ammo hungry! Really, I don't understand the need to scrounge so much. You would think a highly paid mercenary would go in fully equipped. Arrange for supply caches and the like. There are caches but they are usually in enemy control so you cannot access them until after the fight. Seems illogical to me.

 The ballistics are fun with both wind and range to deal with. Adjustable scopes and a computerized mask with different scan modes to help out. HUD also computes wind curves for you so you can pick your hold off. Has a skill/equipment tree you can upgrade with cash you earn from your contracts.

The problems are in the movement system and what to me appears a desire to hang on to pre-open-world player control and direction. Character movement and stealth is impeded by silly errors in design that allow things like a 2 inch lip on a boulder to block a players movement. I have been forced multiple times, in full view of the enemy, to stand and jump to get over tiny level changes in the ground. For example - a two inch lip on a boulder's surface. This has been a problem for some time now and was not fixed by Sniper G.W. Contracts. Game badly needs a parkour system and to get away from manually placed attachment points for jumping and climbing. This plays into the other issue of using old style game practices of controlling the players movement. A open world map is divided up into small sandboxes with limited entry points. The point of open world is to allow the player freedom of movement. Allow the player to pick their own strategic locations and tactical approaches. To improvise their own secret entries and approaches to heavily guarded territory. Instead, as in one example, being forced through the main gate or through a tunnel that dumps you into the lap of a dozen guards, roving patrols and multiple snipers. That isn't exactly the way a stealthy player would approach, at least I wouldn't. How I would dearly love to scale the lofty peaks and find a great sniper hide of my own, but sadly no. Terrain should be varied, but the character's abilities should let them explore most of it. The game also appears to have some stack overruns or cummulative memory errors that build up in a long play session. I have taken to quitting and restarting every hour or two.

Still, don't let this deter you if you like stealth and sniping games. It is a good game overall. It just has those annoying development philosophies and errors which tick me off now and then. Buy now or wait for a sale? I rate this sale worthy.

✅ Positive Features :

1-The game offers a strong focus on authentic sniper experiences, including bullet drop, wind direction, breathing control, and distance calculation. It’s satisfying for fans of precision shooting.
2-Each mission takes place in a semi-open world map, allowing players to approach objectives from multiple angles. You can plan your route, use vantage points, and choose your method—stealth or aggression.

5-The game includes various high-tech tools and gadgets, like drone, remotely-controlled snipe turret , Decoy Trap , Warning Device , grenades and mines

❌ Negative Features :

Differences Between SGWC1 and Earlier games in the Series:

1-Gameplay :
SGWC1 uses a mission-based structure with semi-open sandbox maps. Each mission (called a "contract") is set in a separate, detailed area.
Earlier games (like Sniper Ghost Warrior 3) featured a fully open world, but were criticized for being too empty or buggy.

2-Stealth and Strategy:
SGWC1 focuses more heavily on stealth, careful planning, and tactical decision-making.
Previous titles were more linear or tried to mix open-world elements with traditional shooter gameplay.

3-Customization and Tools:
SGWC1 introduced more customizable gear like masks with special abilities, drones, and advanced gadgets.
Earlier games had more limited equipment and fewer strategic tools.

4-Map Design:
The levels in SGWC1 are dense, replayable, and encourage exploration.
Earlier entries often had more linear paths or less detailed open worlds.

Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts is a dotted line worth signing.

[b]DISCLAIMER: THIS REVIEW DOES NOT EVALUATE MULTIPLAYER MODE DUE TO LOW PLAYER POPULATION.[/b]

[h1]Story[/h1]
Set sometime in the near future, Contracts isn't so much a story as it is a series of things simply happening.  Players don the high tech mask of Seeker, an anonymous contract killer for hire who has entered a deal with an equally anonymous employer to assassinate several high profile targets in the newly formed Siberian Republic.  After a brief but bloody civil war, Siberia has split off from Russia to form its own independent nation.  Under the steady guidance of his contact known only as Handler, Seeker will work his way from target to target and eliminate them all as he goes.  There's very little in the way of characters here.  Handler is curt but professional, keeping most of his conversation on the mission at hand while Seeker is strangely unprofessional in that he simply won't stop asking Handler just who it is that he's working for no matter how many different ways he told to stop asking.  There is a reveal at the end, but the word "reveal" is far too generous for what you get out of it.  It's very clear that the story exists wholly to serve as context for the contract style the gameplay follows, and thus it is utterly devoid of any real merit to speak of.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
An FPS with an emphasis on sniping, SGWC drops players into five different areas of operation.  These maps are by no means open world environments but are each easily a square kilometer in size at a minimum.  Whether it's the twisting blizzard choked crags of Altai-24 or the serene greenery and cliffs of Sibirskaya-7, each map is filled with paths, tunnels, and open fields to navigate and enemies to kill or avoid.  Each area has a primary target for players to assassinate as well as secondary targets and tasks that they can fulfill to earn more cash.  Each map offers its own challenges, bounties, and collectibles to hunt down as well, which in turn, reward points for unlocking different equipment Seeker can use in future jobs.  A plethora of snipers, combat arms, handguns, attachments, gadgets, and abilities can be purchased to give players even more of an edge, though there are many items that feel outright useless compared to others.  You could remove the majority of weapons from the game and nothing would really change for the end user other than shorter menus.  Some upgrades are laughably overpriced for what little they do while other far more game changing abilities come earlier and at significantly less cost.  Each area of the game is filled with outposts large and small and players are given the freedom to tackle these places in any way they wish or even just avoid them.  Although sniping is your best tool as Seeker can fall to just a burst or two of concentrated fire, he's more than capable of holding his own in a stand up fight with the tools he has available if your aim is true.  The sniping itself feels fantastic.  Players can gauge target distance by instant instinct, a brief scope measurement, or taking the time to activate their mask's zoom and tag for the most accurate if slowest method of gauging range.  Meanwhile, the mask itself highlights how wind will affect the bullet at all ranges, but players are free to zero their sight if they wish for a more centered shot.  This ultimately turns sharp shooting into a little minigame all its own that rewards thorough preparation, good measuring skills, or good instincts equally.  Shots well past the 250 meter mark are a joy to watch as their tracer takes over a second to arc down directly into the skull of whichever poor guard you've pulled the trigger on.  Enemies are quick to alert and thus need to be dropped quickly.  If they catch sight of you, hear you, or find evidence of your work; you have mere seconds to silence them before the outpost goes into full alert; though thankfully neighboring outposts won't get the memo.  When inside an outpost, enemies will try to rush, frag, and flush Seeker out until he's dead; and they can be a genuine threat.  On the other hand, if you're sniping from outside, they can do little more than hide behind cover, spray bullets or mortars in your general direction, or be one of the brave few that tries to pull out their binoculars to slowly scan for you.  It's a shame they can't do much more than that but it does make you feel like a lead slinging force of nature that brings entire bases to their knees in fear.  The game can certainly feel repetitive at times and even frustrating when things go wrong in a way that might not feel fair, but overall the sense of freedom, the interconnected nature of the maps, and the solid shooting makes tackling each contract satisfying enough to enjoy doing it all the way to the end.

[h1]Presentation[/h1]
Fantastic but certainly not without deficiencies.  Visually speaking, Siberia's environments are stunning to behold thanks to the game's rich use of vegetation, rock, snow, and lighting.  Despite taking place across one country with mostly samey regional climates, each level feels distinct thanks to their topography and time of day.  Seeker's design stands out as a bit goofy though, and the mask only makes it worse.  He stands out poorly when set next to all of the highly realistic military gear the game surrounds him with.  Sound is equally satisfying to the visuals.  The harsh muted thud of a bullet blasting out of a silenced barrel doesn't get much better than it does here, and the bullet kill cams are simply excellent if a bit drawn out at times.  Animation as a whole is weighty and impactful with the exception of reload animations which feel stiff and awkward.  The music is a bit of a low point.  The game only seems to have a handful of songs which means you'll be hearing the same tracks over and over again.  At best, they're OK, but at worst they quickly become noise that you get tired of hearing and just want to shut off.  Voice acting is solid, though the actors are hardly performing roles that let them truly become a character.

Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts or SGWC (for short) is the perfect game for Sniper enthusiastics.
If you have played a Sniper Elite game this game will feel very similar, however in this one you are forced to stay in a FPS POV. From the start the game will show you different weapons, bullet types and utilities. I do recommend starting a mission and testing it there, instead of the shooting range since a mission has a lot more diversity and will show you how the game works. After completing your first Mission you will get rewarded with credits which you can use to buy new weapons, unlock your skills and utilities. The game has 3 difficulties for each mission. The game rewards you with a slow motion bullet tracker for a precise long shot kill. The only downsides of this game are the following: Sometimes the enemies/cameras/turrets can spot you even though you are clearly hidden. Also sometimes the enemies can immediately notice if there is someone dead even if they are not next to the corpse, which can annoy the player who is clearly going for a stealth walkthrough. There is a "Load from last Checkpoint" option that you can abuse, which makes this game a walk in the park in higher difficulties which kinda annoyed me, but i think this compensates for the bullshit I mentioned before :) . Overall, if you enjoy a sniper based game, you enjoy a stealth/ninja play style and you enjoy using different utilities to approach a mission, this game will suit you well. I finished the game 100% with all achievements in 24 hours but I enjoyed every minute I spent on this game.

- Enemies are super, super, super stupid. They see all their buddies drop like flies when they run around a corner and just run after them anyway. It's a simple sniper game in the Sniper Ghost Warrior series. If you've played any other games from this series, you know exactly what to expect. 

GAMEPLAY?
The sniping is fun, and the bullet cam is satisfying. I like the option to interrogate enemies when approached from behind. Too bad the feature is janky sometimes, the prompt just doesn't show up like the melee kill option. Movement feels a bit...off, you're floaty and the parkour is very stiff feeling, but you get used to it, and most importantly, it works. I do have a big issue with some features like the chain kill skill, the prompt to continue the chain, just doesn't show up, unless the enemies are millimeters away from eachother. Another one is the decoy trap, if thrown nearby, you will alert enemies, completely contrary to  its purpose of remaining stealthy, then the gas trap upgrade just doesn't trigger most to the time. I can safely say I died more to my own gas then the enemies, virtually unusable, which is a shame since the idea behind it is great.
7/10

MAPS?
There are 5 levels (6 if you count the tutorial). All of them are great, I especially like the first and forth ones (i'm a sucker for snowy maps). All of them have alternate routes to objectives, so you can approach them in any way you deem best. My opinion is split on the fast travel system, on one hand its nice not to have to backtrack on foot, but on the other hand sometimes you can entirely skip some challenging areas ([spoiler]worst case is on map 3 at the beginning where you can just skip the stealth segment [/spoiler]). Purely by visuals, the maps look fantastic and really immerses you in the game world.
9/10

SOUNDS?
This game has one soundtrack, and it gets pretty repetitive quite soon (don't get me wrong, the soundtrack is not bad at all). It always starts when you get spotted and engage in combat. There were some occurrences when I didn't get spotted and the game glitched, so it started playing the track through the rest of the mission. Enemies also emit a sound while you're being spotted, which is nice in a semi stealth game like this. Another annoying thing is, every time you look in the general direction of a spotted assassination target it makes a little noise, nice at first, but trust me you'll be hearing it a lot.
7/10

LOADOUT?
It's a simple yet effective inventory screen. You can purchase different weapons with credits and other unlock tokens, which I like, it forces you to play in compliance with challenges so you can unlock more powerful gear. But that is completely negated, since by the end of mission 2 you can afford to have a complete loadout that doesn't have to improve much till the end of the game. In this aspect I think the game is not restrictive enough, it doesn't make you work harder for the better weapons.
The other part of your loadout is your suit upgrades. Most of them you can see their effect immediately, which is a sign of great game design, perks should be very noticeable, not some number that goes up and makes you technically a bit stronger. 
Too bad that some of them just don't work, are effectively useless or are very janky. 
5/10

This is a really good game, and I would also countenance that it has some elements that remind me of playing games in the 'good old days' if you play it on the hardest setting!

[h2]Meat[/h2]
It's very obvious once you start playing that this is based on the Far Cry/Ubisoft dunia (?) engine, and that's a good thing, as it's one of the only ones that allows decent M+K (after some fiddling) and controller to coexist. 

Also good is that it's basically Far Cry bases stringed together with a few loose bits of tiny open world. This is good because you might have noticed that the thing lacking there are any forced 'on rails' elements of gameplay to further the story.

[h2]Two Veg[/h2]
That's because there really isn't much of one (which is fine) because you are a sniper, and you're doing killz, innit.

There's a number of glitches, which because you might need to jump out of some rock you've become Excalibur within, might cause you to be noticed ... this is frustrating ... but I can't remember ever wanting to smash everything and rage quit as a result.

[h2]Pudding[/h2]
So finally on to that hardest setting/ye olde gaming thing. Yes, basically, I'm not a competent gamer, but playing this on hard is really satisfying, because there are none of the previously mentioned forced/on-rails sections with cheap 'gets' for the AI. There's *always* a few ways to get anything done here.

So why is this 'ye olde'? Because I treat raising the alarm (meaning that the enemy has both spotted you, and raised said alarm) as death. So with that comes either a last checkpoint quick reset, or starting the mission fresh. This is ingrained in me from years of FC play, and in old gaming terms ... well, it's like falling down a hole in Mario, or crashing into the trench wall in an Atari Star Wars arcade run. You restart, and you get a TINY bit better (sometimes worse), and play some more.

[h2]A Pair Of Teef[/h2]
So, sure, there's little story, and sometimes you might find yourself talking to the lady in the lake ... but it's engrossing stuff, and you'll find yourself spending hours camped watching patterns, trying to separate two guards that are clearly 'together', or just drinking in the scenery.

Stick it on hardest and enjoy.

If there was a 'mixed' recommendation button I could have selected for this game, I'd have picked it.

Conceptually Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts is very simple: A "realistic" sniping mechanic, a bunch of ducks in a row, and many a high vantage point from which to snipe them to your heart's content. Additionally there's a nice array of gadgets and secondary weapons to play with and upgrade, some of which are very entertaining (turrets, sidearm laser sights, gas mines, and a recon drone to name a few). Charmingly enough, there's also a bona fide RPG layer which adds some much-needed complexity and replayability to what could otherwise end up being a repetitive shooting gallery.

All that being said, the game has some serious, incredibly frustrating flaws. You've probably seen many comments criticizing the janky autosave functionality. These critiques are justified. You'll undoubtedly lose (cumulative) hours of progress since any time you trigger an alert (which is often) the game doesn't autosave unless you exfiltrate, leave the area, or kill literally every opponent in the vicinity.

I'm not seeing as many complaints about the maps, which are admittedly beautifully rendered, but they need be said as well. Objective markers are occasionally unclear, locking onto objective areas on the map seems inconsistent, and there are collision bugs semi-frequently. I had to reload ~3 saves since my character got stuck in a cliff or in a pile of crates. Fall damage killed me many times, and mantling from water to surface is very unreliable. In the frigid waters of Siberia this can result in very unfair deaths, as the game has no way to designate where you can safely clamber out. You guess wrong, you die.

Lack of communication with the player is one of the game's biggest faults, and this is especially apparent when purchasing new weapons. There's no way to preview what attachments or modifications a weapon can undergo, so you'll have to spend money to buy it first. I definitely wasted ~$800,000 on rifles that I didn't know could not be outfitted with my favorite ammunition, bipeds, or scopes.

As an added side note, the enemy's accuracy, even on standard difficulty, definitely breaks immersion. On maps with fewer options for vantage points, this obsoletes any of the game's louder sniper rifles. You'll get spotted after a single shot, and torn apart by enemy automatic rifles even though they're 200+ meters away.

All in all, as a sniper simulator the game excels, and it looks good while doing it. Stray from the formula and you'll likely encounter some resistance. It looks more polished than it actually is, but that doesn't mean it doesn't flow nicely from one encounter to the next. Expect some frustrating moments, but if you're on the fence about buying a cool sniper game that'll occupy your time for 15+ hours, go for it if it's on discount.

This is a stealth sniping game.

The biggest positive this game has is that it is pleasant to interact with.

The negatives are less severe than the positives, but definitely noticeable.
To put it roughly - the game is a bit buggy, especially when loading a save or an area is involved.
It is very clear that the game works on an area-based loading system, there are some predefined areas that, once you enter enemies spawn, and despawn once you leave.
While it is understandable that there is no need to load things that player is not looking at, it should not be this noticeable.
This is further highlighted by the numerous bugs that I noticed without going out of my way that relate just to this loading mechanism, specifically: electronics breaking in sync when you re-enter an area, marks on electronics just vanishing, broken electronics sometimes working despite being broken, drone not triggering the enemy loading so you can scout ahead an empty field only to see it magically spawn enemies once you get close.
The geometry is also a bit bugged, I could constantly hear the "jumped on metal" sound as NPCs kept on getting stuck.
I also got stuck like 3 times and had to reload.
Scout drone jammers feel really buggy - it is not clear where it will work and it seems that sometimes it mixes up whether it is supposed to be jammed or not (area I know should be okay was heavily jammed, jammed area had no distortion and just broke the drone)
Supposedly there are towers that block it, but I could launch near some just fine or had my drone break without any close, it is just confusing.

There is a slight identity crisis where this game can not decide whether it wants to be a "Sniper Ghost" or "Ghost Warrior".
Longest shot I think I got in this game was around 450m and most of them are at around 200-150m range.
That's fine, but at least I would have liked to see some "snipe important target from a kilometer away and get out" kind of deal.
One mission has a challenge of "complete everything with a knife" which implies it is possible to do so and the level has a completion path like that.
That's not bad per se, but the game kinda markets itself as sniper game so I would expect me to challenge on sniping (like kill targets without entering the compound) or stealth (like every level having a "complete everything without alarm", which, admitted one contract had but I would have wanted to see it on all) instead.

To summarize, this is a very decent game.
There is nothing exceptional about it, and it comes across as somewhat bugged, but the gameplay feels good.

If I had to quickly summaries this game, I'd present it as "Far Cry meets Hitman."

Set in a semi-open world, you have five locations in wich you must eliminate a primary target with some secondaries objectives.

In my opinion the game's best strength is its level design, allowing you to choose how to kill your targets. You can snipe them from afar, get close up and stealthily execute them, or go in guns blazing and keep on shooting until the whole map is dead.
The environment is also another strong point, very detailed all while looking really good, and running without any issues.

For the gameplay, you start each mission with 3 weapons (sniper, Assault Rifle and pistol) and a number of gadgets that can be increased via skill points. Unfortunately, guns are rather lacking of personality and I ended up running the one's with the bests stats.
But even then I found shooting to still be satisfying, even if it doesn't hold a candle to games like COD 2019 or Insurgency.

Sound wise, the guns and general effects are good but the music is more of an "ambiance", not an OST that I would ever listen to outside of the game.
And then there's the voice acting. It's ok all around, but there are a few characters that are so over the top, so bad, it's actually good (in a Z movie kinda way)!

There are, however, a couple of negatives: AI and clipping.
Enemies are dumb, no matter the difficulty. They will run around like headless chickens while you pick them off one-by-one, will crouch on the wrong side of cover, etc.
Clipping is mostly an issue when trying to stealth. I have been stuck in front of a branch or by a crack on the ground right next to an enemy a few times too many, resulting in my swift death or alerting the whole level. Very frustrating.

Oh, and there's also a "story" that is completely forgettable and no more than a back drop for the missions.


All around, a good sniping power fantasy with great level design and visuals, somewhat hindered by poor AI and clipping issues.

So I like this game and recommend it though don’t take my long list of cons vs my short list of pros as an indicator.  I’m hard to please.

Pros:

Beautifully designed complex missions with multiple objectives. Though the final mission with radar stations set in deep glacial canyons or microwave antennas aiming at walls makes zero sense. Still, they’re beautiful and engaging to explore.

Bad guys look great. Though the bad guy soldiers and bad guy criminals look and dress exactly the same. Missed opportunity there.

Cool sniper graphics when you make a successful kill. Slow motion bullet graphics depict the actual round fired and not a generic animation for every round (though it is missing the rifling marks). You can also control how often you see this animation from zero to always and anything in between.

Complex external ballistics and wind effects are handled in a way that the player can quickly apply it and understand what is going on. That said, scope reticles in the game are not reflective of real world reticles. In game reticles reflect the distance set when you adjust your range. Sadly, this does not happen in real life (yet?).  Nevertheless, I like it.

Cons:

Can’t save the game. It automatically saves for you but at predetermined checkpoints.  Getting killed often means getting set way back. This is the worst failure in the game, though it does force you to pay attention to your tactics and learn from your mistakes—but that is the problem—it forces you.  It gets exhausting playing the same section over again and that’s often when I quit for the day after losing a great deal of progress.

You have to buy the ability to carry more ammunition but you must choose between sniper rifle and pistol—not rifle—and rifle is what you need the most spare ammo for. And the amount you start with is arbitrary and makes no sense. For example, you start with one magazine in whatever assault rifle you carry (or pick up on the battlefield) and 55 extra rounds. Not two magazines, not three magazines, certainly not four. If your assault rifle carries 20 rounds you still only have 55 rounds on top of that (the equivalent of 2 x 20 round magazines and 1 x 15 round magazine). If it carries 30 rounds you still have 55 rounds extra.  That means one more mag of 30 and one of 25. Must be a game designed by someone who knows nothing about modern firearms and the kit you can wear to carry spare mags. I mean, the bad guys are all wearing it. Why not the player character?

No select fire availability for any of the full auto capable weapons. You fire on full auto all the time. I hate that.

Happily, many of the bad guys carry spare sniper ammo for your particular rifle. Unhappily bodies disappear along with your special ammo you might need. This is often after you reload to a checkpoint or if you leave an area and come back. Though this does have one unexpected advantage. Enemies become alerted if they find a dead comrade but if the body disappears (in spite of his weapon, helmet, or even arms and legs lying on the ground) other guards will not become alerted.

Simplistic ammunition types. There are apparently two types of pistol ammo (light and heavy) and two types of sniper rifle ammunition (also light and heavy). The game hints that some of the pistols are 9mm (not being specific on 9mm short, 9mm Makarov, or 9mm Parabellum) and others are .45 ACP, and .44 Magnum. The 9mm and .45 are considered light pistol ammo and the .44 Magnum is considered heavy pistol ammo. Though the game differentiates about four different sniper rifle cartridge types, it actually categorizes them as light and heavy too. So 7.62 (which is vague as there are numerous rifle cartridges that start with “7.62mm”) and .300 are considered light sniper ammo, while .338 (probably meaning .338 Lapua Magnum) and .50 caliber BMG are considered heavy sniper ammo.

The game does not take into account that finding 5.56mm x 45, .45 ACP, .44 Magnum, and anything outside of 7.62mm x 53R sniper ammo in Siberia would be highly unlikely.

You have to spend all your earnings on buying gear. So instead of your employer outfitting you, you use the money you earn to buy better stuff. Realistically, can you even afford these contract jobs? But then again, what else can you spend your money on? Sigh.

Weapons names are all made up. Every weapon is based on an actual real world weapons but the game is sometimes inconsistent with cartridge types and most definitely inconsistent on magazine capacities and both of these issues are very disappointing. If they’re worried about getting sued, why do they copy the weapon design so exactly that it can be identified for what it is? It is sad that actual magazine capacities are ignored so the game can force you to buy upgrades of larger capacity magazines, which are unrealistically expensive compared to an actual high capacity magazine.

If you pick up better weapons on the battlefield (or one you just like better) they are not available for the next mission. So don’t pick them up as it’s a waste of time.

Weird mask you have to wear which would realistically interfere with your cheek weld. Maybe this is cool for someone else but it’s a silly gimmick. Besides, I’m too old to be cool.

Stupid hood you have to wear. I know it’s the cool factor, but seriously, no one wears those things tactically as it kills your peripheral vision. Yeah, I know. No such thing as peripheral vision in a first person shooter.

Bar graphs to depict weapon stats. I hope I never see another game that does this stupid bar graph to depict weapon stats. Seriously? NOBODY uses that crap in real life! Just tell me the numbers! I want to know the caliber or millimeter of the cartridge, magazine capacity, rate of fire, muzzle velocity, foot pounds of energy, stuff like that. You must have heard of that stuff in your research! No? Look it up. It’s not hard to find.

Scope wobble differs depending on your sniper rifle. This should not an issue with the rifle. It should actually depend on your weapon’s position (standing-worse, kneeling-better, prone-best, supported/bipod-even better).  Once you get in into a good prone supported position, the only scope wobble you will see will be from breathing and your heart beat. Though your shooting position indeed affects scope wobble, the game also makes it very much a sniper rifle characteristic too. If it is really is a weapon issue then your scope mount or rings aren’t tight and you need to fix your rifle because you won’t hit diddly.

Throwing grenades is problematic. When you press your throw button, you don’t see a potential arc of your grenade but rather a bull’s eye on the ground. Which, if you’re throwing up hill or over an obstacle, means you can’t see where your grenade is going so you will probable miss.

No suppressors available for your assault rifle. No suppressor available for select semi-auto pistols  (Gaston 21) which makes no sense. No suppressor available for the revolver either but that is entirely accurate as pistols are notoriously difficult to suppress because of the gap between the cylinder and barrel.

The battery for your super cool drone lasts about 30 seconds. So I’m wondering why I’m carrying it around.

Can’t tag any vehicles. Can’t tag mortars or do any damage to them. You should be able to shoot or destroy the optical sight that the mortar men use for direct lay (when they’re firing at targets they can actually see as opposed to indirect fire). This wouldn’t prevent them from firing at you but it would make them a great deal less accurate or better yet, take them longer to put rounds on your position.

Very good game if you can get over the janky controls and rough terrain. This has really cool sniping mechanics and stealth kill animations, even the climbing is quite cool. But the problem is sometimes the game fights you against what you should be able to move around on, such ledges that take forever to grab on to just because you're not at the right angle to press spacebar yet.

There's also a bloat of gadgets that were either unclear on when best to use them or I just didn't experiment well enough. Though my favourite are the auto sniper turret and the drone even though you could tag enemies faster in binoculars mode.

Despite all this game's faults like the janky controls, awkward terrain traversal, and sometimes really really out of the way challenges you gotta do to get higher scores for more expensive upgrades—I enjoyed this game for the most part despite begrudgingly rushing through the final mission. There's lots of potential for this series to be up in the ranks with other stealth greats like Metal Gear Solid and Splinter Cell. Nice to have a stealthy shooter in first person as it felt really immersive to pull off cool parkour and stealth kills IN first person, ya know, assuming that the janky controls and awkward terrain didn't betray me first.

All in all good game, can't wait to see how part 2 fairs in comparison and if and when we get a part 3 to this series. Would be a good way to end this trilogy better than the original Sniper Ghost Warrior Trilogy where I heard the open world bloat ruined the final game in the entry. Hopefully they've learned from these past five games and deliver us something special!
